A day on Venus is longer than its year.
Venus spins backwards compared with most planets.
Venus is the hottest planet, even though Mercury is closer to the Sun.
Mercury has almost no atmosphere, so its temperatures swing wildly.
Mars has the tallest volcano in the Solar System: Olympus Mons.
Olympus Mons is roughly two and a half times the height of Everest.
Mars looks red because of iron oxide — rust — in its dust.
Sunsets on Mars appear bluish.
Mars has two small moons, Phobos and Deimos.
Phobos is slowly spiralling towards Mars.
Jupiter is more than twice as massive as all the other planets combined.
Jupiter's Great Red Spot is a storm larger than Earth.
Jupiter has the shortest day of any planet, under 10 hours.
Jupiter's moon Ganymede is the largest moon in the Solar System.
Ganymede is bigger than the planet Mercury.
Io is the most volcanically active body in the Solar System.
Europa likely has a salty ocean beneath its icy crust.
Saturn is less dense than water.
Saturn's rings are made mostly of ice chunks.
Saturn's rings are hundreds of thousands of kilometres wide but often only tens of metres thick.
Titan is the only moon with a thick atmosphere.
Titan has lakes and seas of liquid methane and ethane.
Enceladus sprays jets of water ice into space from its south pole.
Uranus rotates on its side, tilted about 98 degrees.
Uranus was the first planet discovered with a telescope, in 1781.
Neptune has the fastest winds measured in the Solar System.
Neptune was found by mathematics before it was seen.
Neptune takes about 165 Earth years to orbit the Sun.
Triton orbits Neptune backwards.
Pluto was reclassified as a dwarf planet in 2006.
Pluto's famous bright 'heart' is a region called Tombaugh Regio.
Pluto's moon Charon is about half Pluto's size.
Ceres is the largest object in the asteroid belt.
The Moon is slowly moving away from Earth — about 3.8 cm a year.
We always see the same side of the Moon.
The Moon has moonquakes.
Footprints left on the Moon could last for millions of years.
Twelve people have walked on the Moon.
Apollo 11 landed on the Moon on 20 July 1969.
The Moon's surface area is a bit less than that of Asia.
A total solar eclipse happens because the Moon and Sun look nearly the same size from Earth.
The Sun makes up about 99.8% of the Solar System's mass.
Sunlight takes about 8 minutes and 20 seconds to reach Earth.
The Sun is about 4.6 billion years old.
The Sun's core is around 15 million °C.
The Sun's outer atmosphere, the corona, is far hotter than its surface.
About 1.3 million Earths could fit inside the Sun.
The Sun is a yellow dwarf star.
Proxima Centauri is the closest star to the Sun, about 4.2 light-years away.
A light-year is a distance, about 9.46 trillion km.
The Milky Way contains a few hundred billion stars.
The Milky Way has a supermassive black hole at its centre called Sagittarius A*.
The first image of a black hole was released in 2019.
The Andromeda galaxy is approaching the Milky Way at about 110 km per second.
Andromeda can be seen with the naked eye from dark places.
The observable universe is about 93 billion light-years across.
The universe is about 13.8 billion years old.
Space is not completely empty; it contains a thin gas of particles.
There is no sound in space because there is no air to carry it.
Astronauts on the ISS see around 16 sunrises a day.
The ISS orbits Earth roughly every 90 minutes.
The ISS has been continuously crewed since November 2000.
Astronauts can grow a few centimetres taller in space.
Yuri Gagarin became the first human in space in 1961.
Valentina Tereshkova became the first woman in space in 1963.
Laika the dog orbited Earth aboard Sputnik 2 in 1957.
Sputnik 1 was the first artificial satellite, launched in 1957.
Voyager 1 is the most distant human-made object.
Voyager 1 left the heliosphere in 2012.
The Voyager probes carry golden records with sounds and music from Earth.
Mirosław Hermaszewski was the first Pole in space, in 1978.
Nicolaus Copernicus, born in Toruń, placed the Sun at the centre of the Solar System.
Comets are made of ice, dust and rock.
Halley's Comet returns roughly every 76 years.
Halley's Comet will next be visible from Earth around 2061.
Shooting stars are tiny bits of space dust burning up in the atmosphere.
The Perseids meteor shower peaks every August.
Meteorites have been found that came from Mars.
Neutron stars are so dense that a teaspoon would weigh billions of tonnes.
Some pulsars spin hundreds of times per second.
Betelgeuse is a red supergiant in the constellation Orion.
Sirius is the brightest star in the night sky.
Polaris, the North Star, sits almost directly above Earth's North Pole.
Stars twinkle because of turbulence in Earth's atmosphere.
Venus is often the brightest object in the night sky after the Moon.
Thousands of exoplanets — planets around other stars — have been confirmed.
The James Webb Space Telescope observes mainly in infrared light.
The Hubble Space Telescope was launched in 1990.
Earth is the only planet not named after a god.
Earth's rotation is slowly getting slower over time.
